extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, scientifically-literate readers, and evaluators of mathematical claims and experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging mathematical demonstrations, experimental estimations, and purported discoveries (including hoaxes and pseudo-solutions) — covering when to trust experiments, how to treat ambiguous data, logical requirements for proofs, and practical checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility / many trials required
rubrics_metrics.description: "In very many trials, then, we may depend upon something like the predicted average."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental estimates should be based on large numbers of trials; repeat an experiment until results stabilize — the author: "This method will hardly be believed until it has been repeated so often that 'there never could have been any doubt about it.'" Example: Buffon's and Ambrose Smith's many-throw experiments used thousands of trials to estimate π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical inference from large samples
rubrics_metrics.description: "from many trials we may form a guess at what the average will be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregate frequency from many trials to approximate the underlying probability/average (law of large numbers). The text illustrates inferring proportions of heads from many coin throws and estimating π from needle trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit handling of ambiguous/undecidable data
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of borderline experimental results affects conclusions (e.g. 11 'contacts on which it was difficult to decide').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how you treat ambiguous cases (split them, count all as hits, exclude them) because different choices materially change estimates (Ambrose Smith example: dividing contacts equally vs treating all as intersections produced different estimates of π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect improbable events given enough trials
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever can happen will happen if we make trials enough."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rare sequences/events (e.g. many heads in a row) will occur with sufficient repetitions; do not treat a single occurrence as proof of impossible or supernatural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept assertions that contradict mathematical demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: "The positive affirmation of that which contradicts mathematical demonstration cannot but be accompanied by a declaration... that demonstration is false."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimant asserting a result that contradicts established proof bears the burden of showing why the proof fails; mere positive assertion is insufficient — evaluate whether the claimant actually refutes the demonstration or merely denies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require proof for converses and reverse claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of claims that "the converses of Euclid... must be necessarily true" without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept the converse of a theorem as true by default; converses require independent proof or explicit limitation. Evaluate arguments that assume converses on their logical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic foundations must be explicitly justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to 'get rid of axioms altogether' or to establish geometry 'without the introduction of any principle not common to other parts' often fail to meet the problem's conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposals change or remove axioms/postulates, demand clear account of what is being assumed or relinquished and rigorous treatment of resulting consequences; be skeptical of works that bypass necessary foundational principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for euphemistic phrasing as a hoax tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: "The skill of the hoax lies in avoiding the words 'quadrature of the circle,' ... speaking of 'the accurate rectification of a circular arc,' which all do not know for its synonyme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware claims that avoid well-known problematic terms by using obscure synonyms; editors and reviewers should check whether novel wording conceals a known impossibility or a pseudo-solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/constructive checks can expose errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Parsey 'might have found out his error by stepping a draughtsman's circle with the compasses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify geometric or constructive claims using standard instruments or elementary constructions where possible; simple practical checks often reveal mistaken reasoning in purported solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor presentation to the validating audience/institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: English public may hear discoveries made 'without mathematics,' while French discoverers seek validation from the Institute of Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present results and evidence appropriate to the community that will judge them: some audiences expect formal proofs and institutional endorsement, others may be persuaded by exposition or experiments; choose venue and style accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective engagement with critics is reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: "No person is bound in reason to enter into controversy with every one who chooses to invite him to the field."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and institutions are not obliged to respond to every challenger; decide when engagement is warranted by the merit of the claim, potential impact, or public confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary mathematical claims require correspondingly strong scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical recurrence of impossible-sounding claims (squaring the circle, overturning Newtonian gravitation) — often asserted by non-specialists or by appeals to revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extraordinary or historically debunked claims with rigorous demand for valid proof and reproducible evidence; be particularly skeptical of appeals to divine revelation, anecdote, or novel informal arguments in place of formal demonstration.
